summary: This program reads a Celsius temperature from the keyboard and keeps asking until the reader types a real number that falls between absolute zero (-273.15) and 100. Once a valid value arrives, it converts it to Fahrenheit and prints the result.

lines.text: A try-with-resources block creates the Scanner that reads the keyboard and automatically closes it when the block ends, so nothing is left open.
The capital-D `Double` is the object version of the number type, which can hold `null` to mean "no valid value yet"; a plain `double` could not.
An intentionally endless loop keeps re-prompting; the only ways out are the `break` below or an exception.
Reading the whole line as text lets the program inspect it before trusting it, and `trim()` removes stray spaces the reader may have typed.
This attempts to turn the text into a number, and throws a `NumberFormatException` when the text is not numeric.
This is the range check: anything colder than absolute zero or hotter than 100 is rejected.
`continue` jumps straight back to the top of the loop so the out-of-range value is discarded and a fresh line is read.
Only a number that passed both the parsing and the range test gets stored.
With a good value in hand, `break` leaves the loop and lets the conversion run.
This catch handles non-numeric text such as "abc" by printing a hint; the loop then repeats naturally.
Java automatically unwraps the `Double` object into the plain `double` the method expects.
A final safety net reports any other failure, such as the input stream ending before a valid number is entered.
Keeping the formula in its own method means the validation loop above stays focused on checking input.
Because `celsius` is a `double`, `celsius * 9` is a decimal value and the division by 5 keeps its fractional part.
